answer:
The FDA will consider overlap in setting a tolerance for a new pigment in cosmetics if the pigment shares a common component with an already-listed colorant, as long as that component is known to cause similar or related biological effects, and in the absence of evidence to the contrary, such components are presumed to have additive toxic effects. The Commissioner will take into consideration the amount of any common component permitted in other color additives, food additives, and pesticide chemical residues, as well as the similar biological activity produced by that substance when establishing tolerances.

21 CFR 70.11(a) states that different color additives may cause similar or related pharmacological or biological effects, and in the absence of evidence to the contrary, those that do so will be considered to have additive toxic effects [1].

21 CFR 70.11(b) states that food additives may also cause pharmacological or biological effects similar or related to such effects caused by color additives, and, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, those that do so will be considered as having additive toxic effects [2].

21 CFR 70.11(c) states that pesticide chemicals may also cause pharmacological or biological effects similar or related to such effects caused by color additives, and, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, those that do so will be considered to have additive toxic effects [3].

21 CFR 70.11(d) states that in establishing tolerances for color additives, the Commissioner will take into consideration, among other things, the amount of any common component permitted in other color additives, in food additives, and in pesticide chemical residues as well as the similar biological activity (such as cholinesterase inhibition) produced by such substance [4].

If FDA grants a petition for a new cosmetic color, the listing regulation will be published in the Federal Register within 90 days after filing of the petition (or within 180 days if extended as provided in section 721(d)(1) of the act). The regulation will list the color additive in part 73 or 74 of this chapter on the appropriate list or lists, and it may specify the conditions under which the color additive may be safely used, including maximum quantities, specific food, drug, or cosmetic uses, methods of addition, and labeling requirements deemed necessary to assure safety. The regulation will only list the color additive for the use(s) for which it has been found suitable and safe; if not, the Commissioner shall by order deny the petition and notify the petitioner of such order and reasons. If the color additive is intended for use in meat, meat food product, or poultry product subject to FMIA or PPIA, the regulation must list any such uses where the color has been found suitable and safe. The regulation may exempt the color additive from batch certification if the Commissioner finds it unnecessary for public health protection, based on considerations of composition, manufacturing process, impurities, toxic potential, control procedures, and variability.

21 CFR 70.3(j) [7] defines "straight color" as a color additive listed in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter, including lakes and substances permitted by the specifications for such color.

21 CFR 71.20(a) [2] requires that the regulation list the color additive in part 73 or 74 of this chapter on an appropriate list or lists as provided under section 721(b)(1).

21 CFR 71.20(a)(1) [3] specifies that the regulation may list the color additive for general use in or on foods, drugs, or cosmetics, or for coloring the human body, and may prescribe conditions such as maximum quantities of straight color or diluent, specific food, drug, or cosmetic classes, methods of addition, and labeling or packing requirements to assure safety.

21 CFR 71.20(a)(2) [4] requires that the regulation list the color additive only for uses for which it has been found suitable and safe; alternatively, the Commissioner may deny the petition with reasons.

21 CFR 71.20(a)(3) [5] mandates that if the color is to be used in meat, meat food product, or poultry product under FMIA or PPIA, the regulation must list such uses where the color has been found suitable and safe.

21 CFR 71.20(b) [6] provides that the Commissioner may exempt the color additive from batch certification if they find it unnecessary for public health protection, based on composition, manufacturing process, possible impurities, toxic potential, control and analytical procedures, and variability of composition.

Yes, shipping test mascaras containing an unlisted color additive to an outside safety lab is permitted under an exemption, provided that the shipment meets specific labeling and recordkeeping requirements. This exemption does not apply unless the conditions in §71.37(a) are met, including that no animals used in such investigations or their products (e.g., milk, eggs) shall be used for food purposes without prior authorization from the FDA based on public health data [1].

The person responsible for shipping or delivering the product must maintain adequate records that include the name and post-office address of the expert to whom the color additive is shipped, the date, quantity, and batch or code mark of each shipment or delivery, and these records must be kept for a period of 2 years after such shipment and delivery [2]. These records must be available for inspection and copying upon request by a properly authorized employee of the FDA at reasonable times [2].

Yes, carmine may be used in a blush product intended for use on the face, including areas near the eyes, as long as it is used in accordance with good manufacturing practices and does not violate any restrictions on use in the area of the eye. However, because the blush contains carmine and is intended for use in or near the area of the eye, labeling requirements apply. The use of carmine in a blush is permitted under 21 CFR 73.2087(b), which allows carmine to be safely used in cosmetics generally, including those intended for use in the area of the eye, provided good manufacturing practices are followed [2]. Additionally, because the product contains carmine and is not subject to the requirements of § 701.3, it must specifically declare the presence of carmine prominently and conspicuously at least once in the labeling, as required by 21 CFR 73.2087(c)(2) [5]. This requirement applies regardless of whether the product is intended for use on or near the eyes, since the term "area of the eye" includes the eyelids and surrounding skin [7].

21 CFR 73.2087(d) exempts batches of carmine from certification because certification is not necessary for public health protection [6].

The FDA can suspend certification service to a company if it appears to the Commissioner that the person has: (1) obtained or attempted to obtain a certificate through fraud or misrepresentation of a material fact; (2) falsified records required to be kept under § 80.39; (3) failed to keep such records, make them available, or allow inventory checks as required by § 80.39; or (4) refused to permit duly authorized FDA employees free access to manufacturing facilities, processes, and formulae involved in the manufacture of color additives and intermediates from which such color additives are derived [1]. The grounds for suspension are specifically listed in 21 CFR 80.34(a)(1) through (a)(4), with each condition being a basis upon which the Commissioner may suspend certification service. A person who contests the suspension has an opportunity for a regulatory hearing before the FDA pursuant to part 16 of this chapter [6].

21 CFR 80.34(a)(1): The FDA can suspend certification service if it appears that a person obtained or attempted to obtain a certificate through fraud or misrepresentation of a material fact [2].  
21 CFR 80.34(a)(2): The FDA can suspend certification service if the person falsified the records required to be kept under § 80.39 [3].  
21 CFR 80.34(a)(3): The FDA can suspend certification service if the person failed to keep such records, make them available, or allow full opportunity for inventory checks as required by § 80.39 [4].  
21 CFR 80.34(a)(4): The FDA can suspend certification service if the person refused to permit duly authorized FDA employees free access to all manufacturing facilities, processes, and formulae involved in the manufacture of color additives and intermediates from which such color additives are derived [5].  
21 CFR 80.34(b): Any person who contests a suspension of service has an opportunity for a regulatory hearing before the FDA pursuant to part 16 of this chapter [6].

answer:
A batch of an FD&C (subpart B) straight color must meet the following general specifications before it can be certified:  
- It must be free from all impurities, except those specifically named in paragraph (b) or in the specifications for that color, to the extent such impurities can be avoided by good manufacturing practice [2].  
- For a straight color listed in subpart B, lead (as Pb) shall not exceed 0.001 percent [5]; arsenic (as As₂O₃) shall not exceed 0.00014 percent [6]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, shall not exceed trace levels [7].  
- For a straight color listed in subpart C or D, lead (as Pb) shall not exceed 0.002 percent [9]; arsenic (as As₂O₃) shall not exceed 0.0002 percent [10]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, shall not exceed 0.003 percent [11].  
- If the straight color contains a barium salt listed in subpart C or D, soluble barium (in dilute HCl) as BaCl₂ shall not exceed 0.05 percent [12].  

The batch must also conform to the general specifications outlined in section (b), which differ based on whether the color is listed in subpart B, C, or D [3], and specifically for subpart B, the limits on lead, arsenic, and heavy metals are as defined above.  

21 CFR 70.3(j) [13] defines "straight color" as a color additive listed in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter, including lakes and substances permitted by the specifications for such color.  

21 CFR 82.5(a) [2] requires that the batch be free from all impurities (other than those named in paragraph (b) or in the specifications set forth therein) to the extent such impurities can be avoided by good manufacturing practice.  

21 CFR 82.5(b) [3] specifies that the batch must conform to the following:  
- For subpart B, lead not more than 0.001 percent [5]; arsenic not more than 0.00014 percent [6]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As) not more than trace [7].  
- For subpart C or D, lead not more than 0.002 percent [9]; arsenic not more than 0.0002 percent [10]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As) not more than 0.003 percent [11].  
- For a straight color containing a barium salt in subpart C or D, soluble barium (as BaCl₂) not more than 0.05 percent [12].  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1) [4] applies specifically to straight colors listed in subpart B and sets the limits on lead, arsenic, and heavy metals as specified in subsections (b)(1)(i), (b)(1)(ii), and (b)(1)(iii).  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(i) [5] requires that lead (as Pb) not exceed 0.001 percent for a straight color listed in subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(ii) [6] requires that arsenic (as As₂O₃) not exceed 0.00014 percent for a straight color listed in subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(iii) [7] requires that heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, not exceed trace levels for a straight color listed in subpart B, except that this limit is subject to the condition that such impurities are not present beyond what can be avoided by good manufacturing practice.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2) [8] applies to straight colors listed in subpart C or D and specifies different limits for lead, arsenic, and heavy metals than those for subpart B.

The regulation requires that FD&C aluminum lakes for cosmetics be prepared by extending a certified water-soluble straight color on an alumina substratum, and each such lake must meet specific composition and specification criteria, including limits on soluble chlorides and sulfates and inorganic matter. The name of the lake is determined by combining the listed name of the parent color with the name of the basic radical (aluminum) and appending the word “Lake.” These lakes are considered straight colors and must conform to specifications set forth for the parent color, including those in §82.50.

21 CFR 82.51(a)(1) [1] requires that any aluminum lake be made by extending a salt derived from one of the certified water-soluble straight colors on an alumina substratum using either the aluminum or calcium basic radical.

21 CFR 82.51(a)(2) [2] specifies that lakes must be prepared from previously certified colors listed in this subpart, and further limits soluble chlorides and sulfates (as sodium salts) to not more than 2.0 percent; insoluble HCl and inorganic matter are limited to not more than 0.5 percent [3].

21 CFR 82.51(b) [4] establishes that each lake made as prescribed in paragraph (a) shall be considered a straight color and listed under a name formed according to specific rules.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(1) [5] requires the name of the lake to include the listed name of the parent color from which it is prepared.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(2) [6] requires the inclusion of the name of the basic radical (aluminum or calcium) combined in the color.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(3) [7] and [8] require that the word “Lake” be appended to the name, as illustrated by the example: FD&C Blue No. 1—Aluminum Lake.

21 CFR 82.50 [9] requires a batch of a straight color (including lakes) to be certified for use in food, drugs, and cosmetics if it conforms to §82.5 and to the specifications set forth in this subpart for that color.

Part 82 requires that an Ext. D&C lake made on a clay substratum using calcium as the basic radical is permitted, provided it meets the specifications for lakes defined under §82.2051. The lake must be prepared by extending one of the straight colors (e.g., Ext. D&C Yellow No. 2) with calcium and applied to a substratum such as clay; however, the specific color or type of lake is not restricted by the substrate alone—only that the preparation follows the general rules for lakes in §82.2051.

21 CFR 82.2051(a)(1) [1] permits lakes made from a straight color (e.g., Ext. D&C Yellow No. 2) extended on substrata such as clay, titanium dioxide, or zinc oxide, provided the lake is formed by combining the basic radical calcium with one of the listed straight colors.

21 CFR 82.2051(a)(2) [2] and [3] require that ether extracts shall not exceed 0.5 percent; soluble chlorides and sulfates (as sodium salts) shall not exceed 3.0 percent; and intermediates shall not exceed 0.2 percent.

21 CFR 82.2051(b) [4] states each lake made as prescribed in paragraph (a) is considered a straight color and listed under the name formed by combining the original color name, the basic radical used, and the word “Lake.”

21 CFR 82.2051(b)(1) [5] requires that the listed name of the color from which the lake is prepared be included in the name.

21 CFR 82.2051(b)(2) [6] requires that the name of the basic radical combined in such color (e.g., calcium) be included in the name.

21 CFR 82.2051(b)(3) [7] requires that the word “Lake” be appended to the name, as in "Ext. D&C Yellow No. 2—Calcium Lake."

21 CFR 82.2050 [8] requires a batch of a straight color (including lakes) to conform to §82.5 and to the specifications set forth in this subpart for such color to be certified for use in externally applied drugs and cosmetics.

No, bithionol cannot be used in the antibacterial body wash, regardless of the level, because bithionol is deemed to render any cosmetic product containing it injurious to users under 21 CFR 700.11(a). The regulation states that bithionol is a deleterious substance and any cosmetic containing it is considered adulterated [1].

21 CFR 700.11(a) prohibits the use of bithionol in cosmetics due to its potential to cause photosensitivity in humans, with possible persistent severe reactions, and risk of cross-sensitization with other chemicals like certain halogenated salicylanilides and hexachlorophene [1].  

21 CFR 700.11(b) provides that regulatory proceedings may be initiated for any cosmetic preparation containing bithionol shipped after March 15, 1968 [2].

(a) Bithionol has been used to some extent as an antibacterial agent in cosmetic preparations such as detergent bars, shampoos, creams, lotions, and bases used to hide blemishes. The tamper-resistant packaging and labeling requirements for mouthwash and vaginal tablets took effect on different dates depending on the product type and specific requirement:

- For mouthwash: The packaging requirement (tamper-resistant package) became effective on February 7, 1983, for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except for the requirement that the indicator or barrier to entry be distinctive by design, which is not specified in this provision [10].  
- For vaginal tablets: The packaging requirement became effective on May 5, 1983, for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date [11].  
- The labeling requirement (including the statement about the tamper-resistant feature) was effective on February 6, 1984, for all affected cosmetic products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except that the specific reference to an identifying characteristic in the label is required only from that date onward [12].  
- For products held for sale after February 6, 1984, the tamper-resistant packaging requirement applies as of that date, even if packaged before May 5, 1983, but this does not apply to the distinctive design requirement [13].

The rule states that the effective dates are tied to when a product is packaged for retail sale and depend on whether it is a mouthwash or vaginal tablet. The packaging requirement applies as of February 7, 1983 (for mouthwash) and May 5, 1983 (for vaginal tablets), while labeling requirements apply with specific dates tied to the type of product and the presence of an identifying characteristic [10][11][12][13].

21 CFR 700.25(e)(1)(i): The packaging requirement for mouthwash is effective on February 7, 1983, for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except for the distinctive indicator or barrier to entry requirement [10].  
21 CFR 700.25(e)(1)(ii): The packaging requirement for vaginal tablets is effective on May 5, 1983, for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date [11].  
21 CFR 700.25(e)(2): The labeling requirements—specifically the need for a distinctive indicator by design and the labeling statement—are effective on May 5, 1983, for all affected cosmetic products packaged for retail sale on or after that date; however, the requirement to reference an identifying characteristic in the label is effective on February 6, 1984 [12].  
21 CFR 700.25(e)(3): The tamper-resistant packaging requirement is effective on February 6, 1984 for products held for sale on or after that date if they were packaged for retail sale before May 5, 1983; this applies to the overall packaging requirement but not to the distinctive design requirement [13].

Each manufacturer and packer who packages a cosmetic liquid oral hygiene product or vaginal product for retail sale shall package the product in a tamper-resistant package, if this product is accessible to the public while held for sale. At entry into the United States, an importer of a finished cream from Europe containing cattle-derived ingredients must affirm that the cream was manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains cattle material and that it was manufactured in accordance with 21 CFR 700.27. If requested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the importer must provide records within five days sufficient to demonstrate that the cosmetic is not manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains prohibited cattle materials. These records must be retained for two years after they were created. The cream may contain tallow provided it contains no more than 0.15 percent insoluble impurities as determined by AOCS Official Method Ca 3a-46 or an equivalent method. No cosmetic shall be manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contain prohibited cattle materials, which include specified risk materials, small intestine of all cattle (except under specific conditions), material from nonambulatory disabled cattle, material from cattle not inspected and passed, or mechanically separated beef. The records required must establish that the cream is not manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains any prohibited cattle materials.

21 CFR 700.27(a)(1) defines prohibited cattle materials as specified risk materials, small intestine of all cattle (except under paragraph (b)(2)), material from nonambulatory disabled cattle, material from cattle not inspected and passed, or mechanically separated beef [2].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(4) defines nonambulatory disabled cattle as those that cannot rise from a recumbent position or walk [7].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(5) defines specified risk materials as brain, skull, eyes, trigeminal ganglia, spinal cord, vertebral column (excluding tail vertebrae and transverse processes), dorsal root ganglia of cattle 30 months or older, and tonsils and distal ileum of the small intestine of all cattle [8].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(6) requires tallow to be produced from tissues that are not prohibited cattle materials or must contain no more than 0.15 percent insoluble impurities as determined by AOCS Official Method Ca 3a-46 or an equivalent method [9].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(1)(i) excludes tallow with no more than 0.15% insoluble impurities, gelatin, hides and hide-derived products, milk and milk products, and materials inspected and passed from a designated country [3].  
21 CFR 700.27(b)(1) prohibits any cosmetic from being manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise containing prohibited cattle materials [13].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(1) requires manufacturers and processors of a cosmetic containing cattle material to establish and maintain records sufficient to demonstrate that the product does not contain prohibited cattle materials [15].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(2) mandates that such records be retained for two years after creation [16].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(6) requires the importer of record to affirm, upon filing entry with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, that the cosmetic was manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains cattle material and was manufactured in accordance with this section; if requested, must provide records within five days demonstrating compliance [17].

answer:
Yes, one ingredient list with "may contain" for colors can cover all 20 shades of eyeshadow sold under one brand, provided that: (1) the product line shares a common trade name or brand designation, and (2) no individual shade has a different brand or trade name appearing in its labeling. This is permitted under 21 CFR 701.3(g)(2)(iii), which allows a single ingredient declaration to apply to all products sold under a common brand if they share the same ingredient list and no distinct brand designation appears on any individual product [3]. Additionally, the list may include "may contain" statements for ingredients not present in the product, as allowed by 21 CFR 701.3(g) [2], provided that such declarations are made only when the ingredient is identified by the phrase “may contain” and all products share a common brand or trade name [3].

21 CFR 701.3(b) requires that the declaration of ingredients appear with prominence and conspicuousness, in letters not less than 1/16 of an inch in height, and may be placed on a tag, tape, or card if space is insufficient on the package [1].  
21 CFR 701.3(g) permits a declaration to include an ingredient not present in the product if it is identified by the phrase “may contain” [2].  
21 CFR 701.3(g)(2)(iii) requires that all products sharing the common declaration must be sold under a common trade name or brand designation, and no individual product may have a different trade name or brand designation in its labeling [3].  
21 CFR 701.3(o)(1) allows for a single list of ingredients common to all products in an assortment (e.g., eyeshadows of different colors), with a statement identifying the other ingredients and specifying which products contain them, provided the list is not misleading and is as informative as practicable [11].  
21 CFR 701.3(o)(2) permits a single ingredient list for products sold together in the same package if the total surface area available for labeling is less than 12 square inches [12].  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to determine whether "may contain" statements can be used for colorants specifically, as no provision addresses colorant presence or absence. However, since the question involves a single brand with multiple shades and common formulation, the conditions in 701.3(g)(2)(iii) and (o)(1) support the use of one ingredient list with "may contain" if all products share the same brand name and no individual shade has a different trade name [3][11].  

Note: The requirement that the declaration must be conspicuous, in letters not less than 1/16 inch, applies generally to all ingredient declarations [1], but does not restrict the use of "may contain" for colorants.

answer:
The labeling exemption for the bulk lotion shipment held at the plant is void ab initio if the cosmetic is mislabeled, as misbranding constitutes a violation that terminates the exemption under the conditions specified in 21 CFR 701.9(d)(1) and 701.9(b). The exemption does not survive once the cosmetic is found to be misbranded during removal from the establishment.

The labeling exemption for a shipment of bulk lotion held at a labeling plant is conditional upon the presence of a written agreement between the person who introduced the shipment and the operator of the establishment where it is processed, labeled, or repacked. This agreement must specify processing, labeling, or repacking details that ensure the cosmetic will not be adulterated or misbranded upon completion of such actions. If the shipment is mislabeled, the exemption becomes void ab initio as a result of the misbranding, per 21 CFR 701.9(d)(1). 

The exemption does not apply if the person who introduced the shipment into interstate commerce refuses to make available for inspection a copy of the written agreement required under paragraph (a)(2), which would cause the exemption to become void ab initio with respect to that person, as specified in 21 CFR 701.9(c). 

The requirement that such an agreement be kept by both parties until two years after the final shipment or delivery from the establishment is mandated under 21 CFR 701.9(a)(2), and copies must be made available for inspection at any reasonable hour upon request, as required in 21 CFR 701.9(a)(2). 

The exemption does not apply if the cosmetic is mislabeled during movement or holding because such misbranding triggers immediate voidance of the exemption under 21 CFR 701.9(d)(1), regardless of whether the agreement was properly executed or maintained.

answer:
The cancer warning rule for coal tar hair dyes applies if the product contains an ingredient listed in 21 CFR 740.18(b), which includes 2,4-diaminoanisole (4-methoxy-m-phenylenediamine) and its sulfate salt (2,4-diaminoanisole sulfate). Since the formulation contains 2,4-diaminoanisole sulfate, it falls under the scope of the rule. The warning must appear on the principal display panel in a conspicuous and readable format as required by §740.2(a), unless an exemption is established under §740.2(b) due to label size limitations.

21 CFR 740.18(a)[1]: The principal display panel of the label must bear the warning: "Warning—Contains an ingredient that can penetrate your skin and has been determined to cause cancer in laboratory animals."  
21 CFR 740.18(a)[2]: This is the specific text of the required cancer warning for coal tar hair dyes containing ingredients listed in paragraph (b).  
21 CFR 740.18(b)[3]: Hair dyes containing 4-methoxy-m-phenylenediamine (2,4-diaminoanisole) or its sulfate salt (2,4-diaminoanisole sulfate) must comply with the requirements of this section; thus, the product in question is subject to the warning requirement.  
21 CFR 740.2(a)[4]: The warning statement shall appear prominently and conspicuously on the label, in bold type on a contrasting background, with letters and numbers not less than 1/16 inch in height, unless an exemption under paragraph (b) is established.  
21 CFR 740.2(b)[5]: If the label is too small to accommodate the warning, the Commissioner may establish an acceptable alternative method, such as smaller type size, by regulation; however, this requires a petition submitted to the Dockets Management Staff for approval.
